alternatives.transcript: For centuries, mapmakers have faced an unavoidable problem, representing a curved planet on a flat surface. Every projection distorts something, whether it is the size of continents, the shape of coastlines, or the distances between cities. The familiar Mercator map, originally designed for navigation, preserves angles but dramatically exaggerates regions near the poles. Consequently, Greenland appears comparable to Africa, although Africa is many times larger. Alternative projections attempt to balance these compromises, sacrificing accuracy in one dimension to improve another. Choosing a map, therefore, is never entirely neutral. It subtly shapes how we perceive the world's geography. Thoughtful readers should ask not only what a map shows, but also what it inevitably leaves out.
